# Measured numbers

Every number here was produced by a command in this repository, on the machine
named next to it. Where a result is unimpressive it is still here.

**The machine.** Apple M-series MacBook Pro, 12 cores, macOS, Java 17. Spark
runs in **local mode against a local filesystem** — not a cluster, not object
storage. Kafka, Redis and MongoDB run in Docker on the same laptop.

**The data.** Events are generated by `scripts/generate_events.py` or by the
test event generator, both of which produce complete session lifecycles rather
than unrelated rows. **They are synthetic.** They are not production traffic and
there is no production traffic to have. Events that really pass through the
service reach the lakehouse the same way — the tee, a broker, the same pipeline
— but the volumes below were replayed, and that is the honest description.

**How to reproduce any of it** is the command under each heading.

---

## 1. Matchmaking: skip-list index against a linear scan

```bash
mvn -pl cloudrelay-service test -Dtest=MatchmakingBenchmarkTest
```

Median nanoseconds per party formed, party size 4, queue held at constant depth
(matched parties are returned to the tail of the queue outside the timed
region, so every measurement is at the stated n). Single threaded, JIT warmed.

| Players queued | Linear scan, O(n log n) | Skip-list index, O(log n + p) | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 255,625 ns | 11,667 ns | 22× |
| 10,000 | 2,798,375 ns | 10,208 ns | 274× |
| 100,000 | 35,576,084 ns | 12,541 ns | 2,837× |

The speedup is not the interesting column. The interesting column is the third
one: it barely moves between a thousand players and a hundred thousand, which is
what O(log n + p) looks like when you plot it. The linear scan grows by a factor
of 139 over the same range.

Both implementations produce the same parties —
`InMemoryWaitingPlayerIndexTest` checks them against each other on randomised
queues — so this is the data structure and nothing else.

The test asserts a 10× floor rather than the measured 2,837×, so a loaded CI
runner does not fail the build while a genuine regression still would.

## 2. Matchmaking: does it produce better games

```bash
mvn -pl cloudrelay-service test -Dtest=MatchmakingBenchmarkTest
```

400 players queued for one game in one region, ratings normally distributed
around 1200 with a standard deviation of 300, arrival times spread over the
preceding two minutes. Party size 4. Rating spread is the gap between the
strongest and weakest player in a party, so lower is a more even game.

| Matcher | Parties formed | Mean spread | p50 | p95 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIFO, arrival order | 100 | 629.3 | 584 | 1024 |
| Skill based, expanding window | 97 | 16.9 | 6 | 53 |

A 97.3% reduction in mean rating spread, for three fewer parties formed out of
a hundred.

**Queue depth is the whole experiment, and an earlier version of this benchmark
got it wrong.** Run at 20,000 queued players the skill matcher scores a mean
spread of 0.1, because at that depth there are roughly eleven players at every
single integer rating and finding three with an identical one is trivial. That
number is real and completely uninformative: it measures the density of the
synthetic population, not the algorithm. A few hundred players waiting for one
game in one region is the situation matchmaking actually faces, and it is where
the two approaches genuinely differ.

## 3. Compaction: the small-file problem

```bash
mvn -pl cloudrelay-lakehouse test -Dtest=CompactionBenchmarkTest
```

A silver table built by streaming ingestion at one file per micro-batch — the
same shape a short trigger interval produces on a live topic. 8,276 events.
Median of 5 runs, one warmup, and the whole benchmark run twice.

| Measure | Before OPTIMIZE | After OPTIMIZE | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Files in table | 50 | 1 | 98.0% fewer |
| Table size | 800.7 KB | 421.1 KB | 47% smaller |
| Average file | 16.0 KB | 421.1 KB | 26.3× larger |

Run B reproduced this to within 0.2%: 50 files to 1, and 800.6 KB down to
420.3 KB. Parquet embeds a little per-file metadata that is not identical
between writes, which is where the fractional difference comes from.

| Query | Run A: before → after | Run B: before → after |
|---|---|---|
| `count_all` | 138.0 → 131.4 ms (1.05×) | 143.5 → 146.5 ms (0.98×) |
| `point_lookup_session` | 172.3 → 138.8 ms (1.24×) | 173.1 → 155.7 ms (1.11×) |
| `game_region_rollup` | 194.7 → 136.6 ms (1.43×) | 224.0 → 203.9 ms (1.10×) |
| `wide_aggregate` | 448.2 → 150.3 ms (2.98×) | 186.7 → 183.1 ms (1.02×) |

Z-ordered by `game_id, session_code`.

**Two runs are shown because they disagree, and the disagreement is the point.**
The file counts came out identical and the byte totals agreed to within 0.2% —
both are read from the transaction log. The query timings did not agree at all:
run B had another JVM competing for the same laptop, and the speedups collapsed
into the noise.

Quoting only run A would be the most natural thing in the world and it would be
dishonest. **The defensible claim from this benchmark is the file count and the
table size, not the speedups.** A `wide_aggregate` that ran 2.98× faster once and
1.02× faster the next time has told you that this laptop cannot measure it, not
that OPTIMIZE is worth 3×.

**Why the timings cannot be trusted here.** The operating system page cache
cannot be cleared between the two phases, so after the "before" phase the data
is warm in RAM and the "after" phase is flattered. Spark's own cache is cleared
between iterations and the reported figure is a median of five runs, which
handles jitter but not a warm cache and not a co-tenant process. Getting a
trustworthy number would need a quiet machine and a dataset far larger than
memory. Neither is available here, so the numbers are reported with the caveat
rather than dressed up.

**What is exact and does hold up:**

- 50 files became 1. The test asserts on this, from the transaction log.
- The table got 47% smaller. That is not compaction moving rows around, it is
  Parquet encoding working better over one large row group than over fifty small
  ones — and it is measured from the log too.
- `count_all` did not improve in either run, which is the control working. It
  reads metadata rather than data, so file pruning has little to save there.

## 4. The analytics tee under a broker outage

```bash
mvn -pl cloudrelay-service verify -DskipUTs=true -Dit.test=AnalyticsTeeIT
```

A real `KafkaProducer` configured exactly as the service configures it, pointed
at a port with nothing listening, so every send blocks for the full
`max.block.ms`.

| Measure | Result |
|---|---|
| 200 session publishes against a dead broker | under 2,000 ms total for the caller |
| Exceptions reaching the caller | 0 |
| Events silently lost with no counter incremented | 0 |

Under 10 ms per publish, against a producer that would otherwise block for two
seconds on each one. That is the bounded executor doing its job.

The same test against a live broker publishes a burst of 300 events with zero
dropped, and asserts the JSON on the topic parses into the shape the lakehouse
declares.

## 5. Exactly-once, across a crash

```bash
mvn -pl cloudrelay-lakehouse test -Dtest=ExactlyOnceRestartTest
```

These are correctness results, so they are pass/fail rather than measurements.
They are the most valuable numbers on this page anyway, because a throughput
figure only means something once the counts are known to be right.

| Scenario | Assertion |
|---|---|
| Bronze killed after 2 of 60 micro-batches, then restarted | Final row count equals the events produced exactly; every raw payload appears once |
| Silver killed mid-stream, then restarted | Row count and the set of `event_id`s both equal what was produced |
| Producer retries: every event duplicated adjacent to its original | Bronze keeps both copies; silver holds exactly one per `event_id` |
| Producer retries arriving many micro-batches apart | Same — this is the case the watermark version failed |
| Whole pipeline re-run over a consumed source | Nothing added, to any table |

## 6. A watermark that lost 96% of the data

This one is a bug, measured, and it is on this page because it is the most
useful number in the project.

Deduplication was originally
`withWatermark(...).dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark("event_id")`, which is the
documented approach. Replaying a backlog at one file per micro-batch:

| Stage | Rows |
|---|---|
| Ingested into bronze | 8,276 |
| Reached silver | 354 |

95.7% of the data was discarded as late-arriving, silently, with no failure
anywhere. The watermark jumps to near the maximum event time on the first batch,
and from then on most events are behind it.

The fix was to move the identity check out of Spark's state store and into a
Delta MERGE on `event_id`. After the change, the same replay lands all 8,276
rows, and
`ExactlyOnceRestartTest.duplicatesArrivingInSeparateBatchesAreStillDeduplicated`
exists specifically to stop it regressing.

## 7. End-to-end pipeline

```bash
python3 scripts/generate_events.py --sessions 8000 --files 120
./scripts/lakehouse.sh run --source file
```

32,619 events from 8,000 session lifecycles, through bronze, silver and all four
gold tables:

| Table | Rows |
|---|---|
| `bronze_session_events` | 32,619 |
| `silver_session_events` | 32,619 |
| `silver_quarantine` | 0 |
| `gold_session_lifecycle_1m` | 1,808 |
| `gold_region_concurrency_1m` | 479 |
| `gold_session_duration` | 8,000 |
| `gold_matchmaking_funnel` | 16 |

Bronze equals silver because the generated events are all well formed; the
malformed cases are exercised deliberately in `DataQualityTest`. The gold
counts reconcile against what the generator produced — 8,000 sessions, and 16
game-and-region pairs from four games across four regions — which is what
`MedallionPipelineTest` asserts on every run.

## What is deliberately not claimed

- **No cluster numbers.** Everything is local mode on one laptop against a local
  filesystem. The code is unchanged on a cluster against object storage — that
  is what the Delta log is for — but unchanged in principle is not the same as
  measured, and it has not been measured.
- **No sustained events-per-second figure for the streaming pipeline.** Wall
  clock for a replay is dominated by driver startup and by per-batch overhead at
  these volumes, so dividing rows by seconds would produce a number that says
  more about JVM startup than about throughput. A figure worth quoting needs a
  cluster and a sustained load, and neither is available here.
- **The MERGE-based deduplication in silver gets more expensive as a partition
  grows**, because each micro-batch joins against the partition it is writing
  into. Periodic `OPTIMIZE` is what keeps that bounded, which is why compaction
  is part of the design rather than optional housekeeping. A clean measurement
  of that curve needs an uncontended machine and has not been taken, so no
  number for it appears here.
